title: Reading: Xenophon, Anabasis I.1.1–11
subtitle: Your first unadapted Greek prose.
objectives: Read, parse, and translate the opening of Xenophon's Anabasis without adaptation.
Recognize and apply all the grammar learned in Stages 1-3.
Understand the narrative style and vocabulary of Xenophon.
Build confidence for reading sustained Greek texts.

sections.heading: The opening of the Anabasis
sections.body:
Xenophon's Anabasis is the classic Greek prose text for intermediate readers. The opening lines introduce Cyrus the Younger and his two sons. The syntax is clear, the vocabulary is accessible, and the narrative is gripping.

This is unadapted Greek. Every word is as Xenophon wrote it. The passage is glossed and annotated, but the Greek is real. Read it aloud first, several times, before working through the translation. Let the sound of the language settle in your ear.

This is the moment you have been preparing for. You can read Xenophon.

sections.heading: Anabasis I.1.1-2 (excerpt)
sections.body:
Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος γίγνονται παῖδες δύο, πρεσβύτερος μὲν Ἀρταξέρξης, νεώτερος δὲ Κῦρος. ἐπεὶ δὲ ἠσθένει Δαρεῖος καὶ ὑπώπτευε τελευτὴν τοῦ βίου, ἐβούλετο τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω παρεῖναι. ὁ μὲν οὖν πρεσβύτερος παρὼν ἐτύγχανε· Κῦρον δὲ μεταπέμπεται ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἧς αὐτὸν σατράπην ἐποίησε, καὶ στρατηγὸν δὲ αὐτὸν ἀπέδειξε πάντων ὅσοι εἰς Καστωλοῦ πεδίον ἁθροίζονται.

Gloss:
Δαρείου — of Darius (gen. sg.)
καὶ — and
Παρυσάτιδος — of Parysatis (gen. sg.)
γίγνονται — are born (3rd pl. pres. mid. of γίγνομαι)
παῖδες — sons (nom. pl.)
δύο — two
πρεσβύτερος — elder (comp. adj., nom. sg. masc.)
μέν — on the one hand (particle)
Ἀρταξέρξης — Artaxerxes (nom. sg.)
νεώτερος — younger (comp. adj., nom. sg. masc.)
δέ — on the other hand; but
Κῦρος — Cyrus (nom. sg.)
ἐπεὶ δέ — and when
ἠσθένει — was sick (3rd sg. imperf. of ἀσθενέω)
Δαρεῖος — Darius (nom. sg.)
ὑπώπτευε — suspected (3rd sg. imperf. of ὑποπτεύω)
τελευτήν — end (acc. sg.)
τοῦ βίου — of life (gen. sg.)
ἐβούλετο — wished (3rd sg. imperf. mid. of βούλομαι)
τὼ παῖδε — the two sons (acc. dual)
ἀμφοτέρω — both (acc. dual)
παρεῖναι — to be present (pres. inf. of πάρειμι)
ὁ μέν οὖν — therefore on the one hand
πρεσβύτερος — the elder
παρών — being present (pres. part. of πάρειμι, nom. sg. masc.)
ἐτύγχανε — happened to be (3rd sg. imperf. of τυγχάνω)
Κῦρον δέ — but Cyrus (acc.)
μεταπέμπεται — he sends for (3rd sg. pres. mid. of μεταπέμπομαι)
ἀπό — from (+ gen.)
τῆς ἀρχῆς — the province (gen. sg.)
ἧς — of which (gen. sg. fem. relative pronoun)
αὐτόν — him (acc.)
σατράπην — satrap (acc. sg.)
ἐποίησε — he made (3rd sg. aor. of ποιέω)
καὶ ... δέ — and also
στρατηγόν — general (acc. sg.)
ἀπέδειξε — he appointed (3rd sg. aor. of ἀποδείκνυμι)
πάντων — of all (gen. pl.)
ὅσοι — as many as (rel. pron., nom. pl. masc.)
εἰς — into (+ acc.)
Καστωλοῦ πεδίον — the plain of Castolus (acc.)
ἁθροίζονται — assemble (3rd pl. pres. pass. of ἁθροίζω)

Translation:
Of Darius and Parysatis are born two sons, the elder Artaxerxes, the younger Cyrus. And when Darius was sick and suspected the end of his life, he wished both his sons to be present. The elder, then, happened to be present; but Cyrus he sends for from the province of which he had made him satrap, and he also appointed him general of all who assemble in the plain of Castolus.

sections.heading: What you have done
sections.body:
You have read Xenophon. The opening of the Anabasis is the first sustained Greek prose that most students read, and you have read it. The grammar is complex: genitive absolutes, aorist participles, dual forms, indirect statement. But you recognized it all, because you have learned it.

This is the threshold. From here, you can read any Greek prose with a lexicon and a grammar. The rest is vocabulary and practice.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Answer these questions without looking back.

items.prompt: Who are the two sons of Darius?
Why does Darius send for Cyrus?
items.answer: Because Darius is sick and suspects the end of his life, and he wishes both sons to be present.

items.prompt: What position had Darius given Cyrus?
items.answer: Satrap of a province and general of all who assemble in the plain of Castolus.

items.prompt: What is the case of Δαρείου?
What is the tense and voice of γίγνονται?
What is the mood of παρεῖναι?

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 3.15 is the second sustained reading: John 1:1-18, the Prologue to the Gospel. This is Koine Greek, not Attic, but the grammar is almost identical and the vocabulary is simpler. After this lesson you will have read both Attic prose and Koine, and you will be ready for Stage 4.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can read the passage aloud with accurate pronunciation and can translate at least 80% of it without consulting the gloss.
